“EnvHarness: Awakening Static Worlds for Agent Learning”

Agent environments are usually static, so they quickly stop teaching an improving agent anything new.

This paper wraps existing environments with programmable components that modify states, interactions, and task structure without changing the underlying environment or verifier.

EnvRigger then watches agent rollouts, diagnoses weaknesses, and automatically reshapes the environment around them.

This improves held-out performance by up to 9 points while also reducing execution steps.

https://t.co/weou32qk4J

"Your Agents Are Not Time Aware"

Ironically, coding agents are measured by how long the tasks they are automating would take a human to solve, but we rarely ask whether the agents themselves know how long they have been working.

This blog basically has Claude Code and Codex predict their own wall-clock runtime before a task and estimate it afterwards.

Both agents consistently over-predict, tending to guess around an hour and a half even when tasks take only minutes.

Their actual runtime is also heavily shaped by the harness: Claude Code keeps working much longer, while Codex often stops early.

https://t.co/koHAoii0ue

Quick heads-up that Depth Anything V4 was withdrawn after its central claim was found to be false.

The issues go beyond reproducibility and include fundamental inconsistencies in the paper itself. We take scientific integrity seriously and are sorry for having shared it.

Please don’t use the paper as reference material.

tweets.text:
How can you trust @Bot​s to operate autonomously?

This is something we've carefully designed. First, we use an LLM to automatically review every action your bot takes. If anything is unexpected, it will ask for your approval.

But this isn't enough. We also have customizable rules to allow or deny actions. For example, I have bots that are connected to my X, Gmail, etc. I explicitly block any write/destructive actions and have it ask for my approval first.

This is a good balance between YOLO mode and reviewing everything by hand. Although, we do support YOLO if you like to live dangerously!

How to build great evals - part 6

Hill climbing on evals is just a fancy way of saying: pick a dimension that matters and optimize for it.

This could be improving the quality of existing features based on your latest production data on high value user journeys, expanding to adjacent use cases, lowering cost or latency.

The actual work boils down to better harnesses and model selection through methods like prompt eng, context eng, memory, post training, deterministic old school code etc.

Your failure mode taxonomy (from part 3) is a good compass for where your product struggles and needs some love.

E.g. maybe tool calling failures are your most common problem. You dig in and notice you stuff 20 tools in context, when each task really only needs 3-5. hill climbing here involves context eng to give it the right tools at the right stage and iterate until you get it to good.

Or take the cost reduction goal..
I’ve written about how I advise launching your product with the best model first. Get the quality as high as you can. Once you know users love the experience, hill climb to get similar quality with a smaller, cheaper, faster model. Same methods - harness, models.

The important thing is to have evals that tell you whether you are actually moving in the right direction.
